The line discusses R. Eliezer ben Yaakov excluding a robber's house from those who return from battle, and Rambam 7:5 codifies this ("או הגוזל בית, הרי זה אינו חוזר"), while 7:3 only describes the order of the priest's announcements.
The line quotes "כשדה החרם" (Lev 27:21) directly and discusses R. Yehuda ben Beteira's proof verse "כל חרם קדש קדשים" (27:28), so the margin's citation of A is acceptable.

ref: Mishneh Torah, Admission into the Sanctuary 1:6

judge.reason: The Gemara line quotes Rabbi's view that priests are always forbidden wine but 'his repair is his ruin', which Rambam 1:7 codifies ("תקנתו קלקלתו", a priest who knows neither his mishmar nor his beit av may drink always), while 1:6 covers only the mishmar's nights versus days.
Passage A (SA OC 147:1) rules that the greatest of those who read from the Torah furls the scroll, which is exactly what this Gemara line says, while B is about positioning the scroll at the seam.
The line quotes Leviticus 17:13 ('ושפך וכסה') and also Leviticus 17:12 ('ואמר לבני ישראל'), so the margin's citation of 17:12 is acceptable.

The line distinguishes seed sown in sanctity from seed not sown in sanctity, which is the exact language of Rambam Divorce 11:21 (B); A only concerns counting the waiting period from the date the get was written.
The line quotes 'lo tissa' (Exodus 20:7), the prohibition on taking God's name in vain, and Exodus 20:6 about showing kindness to those who love Him is not discussed.
The line quotes Genesis 17:15 (name change from Sarai to Sarah) and then 17:16 ('וברכתי אתה...'), so the margin's 17:15 is correct and 17:16 is also quoted.

The line concerns Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling that the halakha follows Isi ben Yehuda, who holds that a runner who damages is liable, and Shulchan Arukh 378:8 codifies exactly that: a runner who injures a walker is liable, with the Friday-twilight exception drawn from the same sugya.

The line is about a debtor who attributes his money to a gentile and is forced to sell land; B states this directly, and A (101:1) also mentions 'תלה מעותיו בעכו"ם' in its heading and the rule that a liar must go and sell, so A is acceptable.

The line discusses a declaration of duress (modea) made before two witnesses without needing to say 'write it', which matches SA 205:1 on delivering a modea before two witnesses; 205:8 covers a different case, a robber's sale.

The line cites the mishna in Kilayim that a se'a containing a quarter-kav of another kind must be reduced before sowing, which Shulchan Arukh YD 297:5 codifies (mixed seeds must be reduced before sowing), whereas 296:5 deals with seeing kilayim in another's vineyard.
The quoted phrase "עד חדש ימים" appears in Numbers 11:20 (B), not in 11:19 (A), which only lists days up to twenty.
The line quotes 'באש ישרף' about burning leftover sacrifice, which appears in Leviticus 19:6, while 19:7 concerns eating on the third day (piggul).

Sotah 8b:13-14 is a parallel to Ketubot 30a-30b: Passage A has Rav Yosef's statement in the name of R. Chiyya and the question 'but they have ceased', and Passage B continues with the answer and the four deaths, so A, which the margin cites, is acceptable.

The Gemara line discusses whether Shabbat limits (techumin) apply above ten handbreadths, which is the subject of Rambam Sabbath 27:3, while 26:3 deals with moving potsherds and jar stoppers and is unrelated.
The line is about the blood of a live nine-month fetus found in a slaughtered animal, which Rambam 6:5 addresses directly, while 6:4 never mentions a fetus.
The Semag passage covers kiddushin law and cites Kiddushin 62b ('האומר' ch. 3, daf 64), but it never mentions Rav Oshaya's case of betrothal 'after I divorce you', so it does not codify this line.

The Gemara line states that a competent man who marries a deaf-mute or psychotic woman and writes her 100 manah has a valid ketubah because he chose to harm his property, which is exactly SA 67:9; 67:8 covers the general rule that no ketubah was enacted for her.

The line is Mishnah 3:3 on the willow branch (B), but A is the parallel Mishnah on the lulav with the same clauses (stolen, dry, asheira, ir hanidachat, top severed, leaves split off), so a Mesoret HaShas cross-reference to it fits.

Rambam 6:6 codifies the same two cases: if the seller says 'when you bring the rest you will acquire,' the seller may eat the produce and the buyer may not, and if he says 'acquire from now and the remaining money is a debt with you,' the buyer may eat and the seller may not.
The Chullin derivation "mah chatat behemah einah ba'ah ela min hachulin, uveyom, uveyado hayemanit" begins at the end of A and finishes in B, so the parallel spans both and A is acceptable.

ref: Mishneh Torah, Murderer and the Preservation of Life 6:6

judge.reason: The line's resolution is demolishing into a garbage dump (לאשפה) where people are not found, which is the case Rambam 6:7 addresses, while 6:6 covers only the public domain.
Passage A rules that a relative is lowered into the fields of a missing person, which is the Rav/Shmuel dispute, while B only covers exceptions (minors, a relative through a relative).

Passages A and B are one continuous Pesachim discussion that quotes the same mishna (half-slave half-free, Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai, 'lo tohu bra'), so the citation to A fits and B is only its continuation.

judge.reason: The Mishna's list includes rova/nirba/muktzeh/ne'evad (B) as well as etnan and mechir (A), so both Rambam passages restate parts of it.

The baraita says one may not buy strands from a carder, but one may buy a cushion full of strands, and this is exactly what Passage B (358:12) rules, while Passage A only states a general rule to follow local custom.

The Gemara line quotes the baraita that bee honey is permitted because bees only bring nectar into their bodies and do not excrete it, and Tur Yoreh De'ah 81 codifies this ruling ("דבש דבורים מותר") together with the donkey urine and other excretion laws.

The line quotes the prohibition 'lo tachmod' with the words 'ishet re'acha ve'avdo ve'amato...', which appear in Exodus 20:14, while 20:13 has murder, adultery, theft and false witness and contains no coveting.
The line quotes Numbers 9:11 ('al matzot u-merorim yochluhu') and 9:12 ('ve-etzem lo yishberu bo'), so the margin's citation of A (9:12) is acceptable.

Passage A ends by quoting the opening of the mishnah (הלוקח יין מבין הכותים), which matches line 28a:16, and Passage B continues the same quotation, including the Rabbi Yehuda, Yosei and Shimon prohibition of 28a:17, so A is acceptable.
The Gemara quotes both Leviticus 25:13 and the juxtaposed 25:14 ('וכי תמכרו ממכר'), so the margin's citation of 25:14 is acceptable.

The Mishnah speaks of offerings made in a (cooking) vessel, the pan and deep pan, and Rambam 13:6 gives exactly that case with its three oil placements, while 13:5 covers the plain fine-flour offering.

The line's baraita says that if he says 'deliver a bill of divorce,' one person delivers on behalf of all, which is what Passage A rules. Passage B covers the 'whoever hears my voice' case of writing, which is not discussed here.
The line quotes both Leviticus 22:10 ("וכל זר לא יאכל קדש") and 22:12 ("בת כהן... בתרומת הקדשים"), so the margin citing 22:10 is correct.
The line is about 'like cherem' (heavenly vs. priestly, unspecified forbidden), which is exactly Rambam 2:8; passage A concerns maaser, a different case.
The Gemara quotes Psalms 148:7-8 as one continuous citation, and the items it needs (תנינים, תהומות in 7; אש, ברד, שלג, קיטור in 8) are split across both verses, so A is acceptable.
The line quotes both Numbers 15:13 ("אזרח") and Numbers 15:11 ("ככה"), so the margin's citation of A is acceptable.

The line quotes Rav's rule that a woman may be secluded with two men in town but on the road needs three, and Shulchan Arukh EH 22:5 codifies exactly this (two in town, three in the field or at night), while 22:8 concerns a woman whose husband is in town.
The line quotes Leviticus 26:30 (ונתתי את פגריכם) and 26:31 (והשמותי את מקדשיכם) in succession, so A is acceptable.
The line opens the four-shaving list with the first shaving's birds; A covers the birds brought at the shavings and B lists the four shavings, so both fit.

The Gemara line is about human blood on bread versus blood between the teeth, and Passage B quotes it directly ('וחילופא בדם... שבין השינים מוצצו'), while Passage A deals with sexual conduct and never mentions this ruling.

judge.reason: The line covers the sprinklings on the golden altar's corners and middle (Passage A) and also the pouring of the remaining blood on the western base (Passage B), so A is acceptable.
The line quotes both Numbers 13:27 ("ויספרו לו ויאמרו באנו") and 13:28 ("אפס כי עז העם"), so the margin's citation of 13:28 is acceptable.
The Gemara quotes Haggai 2:11-12 together, and the steinsaltz cites 2:11-12; verse 11 is the introductory 'ask the priests' and verse 12 holds the quoted content, so A is acceptable.
The line explicitly quotes 'ובכתה את אביה ואת אמה', which is in Deuteronomy 21:13, not in verse 12.
The line quotes the mishnah about drinking (וישתה), bringing head and most of the body in, and 'וכן בגת', which is Mishnah 10:6; passage A concerns urinating and spitting.
The line quotes the mishna on a non-kosher bird on kosher eggs (Passage B) and infers the kosher-on-kosher case, including a different species, which Passage A rules on.

The Mishna on the anointed priest's ruling, 'הורה בפני עצמו... מתכפר עם הצבור', and the rule that a court is liable only if it nullifies part and sustains part, appear in Passage B (Semag 217). Passage A covers the oleh veyored offering and does not mention them.
The baraita quoted (female designated for Pesach grazes until blemished, sold; if she bore a male it likewise grazes and is sold) matches Tosefta 9:9 almost verbatim, whereas A deals with temurah.
The Mishnah's rule that the thigh is forbidden if the nerve imparts flavor (בנותן טעם) matches A's general notan-taam ruling, while B concerns recognizable versus unrecognizable nerves.
The Gemara quotes Zechariah 2:8 directly, and Steinsaltz's English cites 2:7–8 because the quotation opens with the angel going out in verse 7, so A is acceptable.

The Gemara lists hands to be severed for touching the eye, nose, mouth, ear, wound and anus; A (SA 4:4) codifies the anus and wound items, and B (4:3) codifies the eye, nose, mouth and ear items, so both are drawn from this line and A is acceptable.

judge.reason: The Mishna has two rulings: shoshvinut is collectible in court and returns to the middle (Passage A, 7:13), and jugs of wine or oil are not collectible because they are acts of kindness (Passage B, 7:15), so both fit and A is acceptable.

The Gemara line is the Mishnah of the woman who went overseas with her husband and son, and Passage B repeats it nearly word for word (Mishnah Yevamot 15:8), while Passage A is the separate case of a woman who returns and says her husband died.
The line explicitly quotes 19:28 'וירגל בעבדך אל אדני המלך ואדני המלך כמלאך האלהים', while 19:26 is not quoted here.

judge.reason: A matches the night-immersion of a lesser zava being invalid, and B matches the woman who sees on day eleven, immerses at evening and defiles lying and sitting; A is acceptable.
The line quotes 'ככה תעשו לאחד', which appears only in Numbers 15:12 (Passage B); Passage A has 'ככה יעשה לשור האחד' and lacks that phrase.

The line quotes 'מי יתן והיה לבבם זה להם ליראה אותי כל הימים', which is Deuteronomy 5:26 (Passage B), while Passage A has no such text; the Steinsaltz citation of 5:26 confirms it, though the English translation says 5:25.
The same mishna quote (כל הכלים יורדין לידי טומאה במחשבה...) begins at the end of A and continues into B, so A is acceptable.

judge.reason: The Mishna's rule that proof overturns the verdict, with the 30-day limit, is codified in Rambam 7:6 (B), while 7:7 (A) covers the later sealed-claims case.
B restates the Mishna's three prohibited types, while A restates the vine-products and olive-bulk (kezayit) liability that the line also contains.
The line says the seven red-heifer sprinklings are each essential, and Rambam 4:7 rules that lacking one sprinkling invalidates the heifer, while 4:9 deals only with night sprinkling.

The Gemara line is about smearing oil and rubbing the intestines on Shabbat, while the cited Semag passage covers the prohibition against profaning one's daughter into prostitution, so the two are unrelated.
The Gemara quotes Psalms 34:13-14 together, opening with 'Mi ha-ish he-chafetz chayim' (v.13) and continuing with 'netzor leshonkha' (v.14), so the margin's citation of v.13 is acceptable.
The line states that new and old animals are not tithed for each other (Rambam 7:5) and derives from "וצאן" that sheep and goats are tithed together (Rambam 7:4).
The Gemara line discusses why a deaf-mute woman married to a priest may not eat teruma, which is the ruling in Passage B; Passage A, on a non-priest eating teruma deliberately, is unrelated.
The line infers the rule from 'the get comes out from under both their hands,' which Rambam 7:15 states explicitly, while 7:14 does not use that distinction.
A codifies the eternal prohibition on Netinim, while B has the Gibeonite decree covering males and females; both match parts of the Mishnah, so A is acceptable.

Passage B quotes the mishna's 'Rabbi Elazar says: we teach the minor to refuse him', while A deals with 'halakha like Rabbi Eliezer' on other matters.

The line explicitly quotes Numbers 25:12 ('Therefore say: I hereby give him My covenant of peace'), and its closing comment on atonement draws on 25:13 ('he atoned for the children of Israel'), so the margin's A is correct and B also fits.
The Gemara line states both the craftsman (A, 13:4) and the sharecropper (B, 13:6) descending from their positions and gaining chazakah, so both rulings derive from it and the cited A is acceptable.
The line (cow gives birth, ewe sheared, robber pays at the time of robbery) is codified in Tur 354, which opens with this exact case; Tur 353 covers change of name and owner's despair.
The line's closing rule that a doubtful firstborn is eaten in its blemished state by the owner opens Tur 315, and Tur 318 codifies the specific prior-birth cases of the same sugya.

judge.reason: The line is about a deathbed husband saying 'give 200 zuz to my wife as is appropriate for her', and Passage B restates exactly that; Passage A only covers the firstborn's share.
The Gemara explicitly quotes the Mishnah at the end of Makkot (20a), 'liable on the head for two, one from here and one from there', which is the text of this cited passage.

The line discusses a convert who converts on Passover eve and Beit Hillel's view that he is like one separating from a grave, which is the ruling in Rambam Paschal Offering 6:7; passage A, about breaking the bone of the fat tail, is unrelated.

The Gemara line has Rava saying a person cannot make himself wicked, so testimony that someone sodomized him willingly is split and combines with another witness; SA 34:26 states this ruling, while 34:27 covers a different case of one who swore to deny a witness.

The Gemara case is a man who snatched a silver ingot before one witness and said 'I snatched what was mine', which is exactly Passage B (364:4), whereas A covers a general one-witness case with claims of purchase or deposit.

The Gemara says to recite Shehecheyanu when making a lulav or sukkah for oneself, and Rambam 11:9 lists sukkah and lulav as mitzvot that take Shehecheyanu, with a fallback when it is not said at making; B only covers the general rule that Shehecheyanu applies to a mitzvah done for oneself.
A states the no-intent principle the Gemara asks about, while B codifies the mishna's deaf-mute, psychotic and minor slaughtering under supervision, so both fit and A is acceptable.
The Mishnah's first clause (slaughtering for an individual) is codified in A, and its last clause (a group of a hundred unable to eat a k'zayit) is codified in B, so the cited A is acceptable.

The Gemara line discusses R. Yoshiya's rule of sowing wheat, barley and a grape pit 'במפולת יד', and Passage A states this same rule (two kinds with the grape pit במפלת יד); Passage B concerns when produce becomes sanctified and does not mention it.

judge.reason: The line states both the general retroactive impurity of stains (A) and the exception of 'dayan sha'atan' women whose stain equals their sighting (B's opening).
The line has two rulings: torn intentionally or accidentally, which matches A's torn-document law, and erased or smudged with a recognizable imprint, which B quotes almost verbatim.

The line gives the shehiyah measure of lifting, laying down and slaughtering; A states this measure generally, and B adds the small-versus-large distinction (דקה לדקה וגסה לגסה) that the line also states, so both fit and A is acceptable.
The line quotes "איש כאחיו", which is in Leviticus 7:10 (A); the "ואם על תודה" clause is in 7:12, so B (7:11) is not the quoted verse.

The Mishnah line disputes whether cursing parents with divine appellations (not the ineffable name) is capital, and Rambam 5:2 codifies the Rabbis' view that only the ineffable name incurs stoning while an appellation is exempt; B concerns cursing grandparents, which this line does not address.

The Gemara covers a man who says he married a woman overseas and must prove her lineage but not the children's, and with two wives must prove both. Passage B (20:7) restates exactly this, while A covers a different case where the wife left with him and is already known to be fit.

The Gemara line asks whether the shehiyya (interruption) measure is the duration of slaughtering an animal for an animal and a bird for a bird, and Passage A sets exactly those shiurim for birds and animals, while Passage B covers a dull knife and does not fit.
The line quotes Numbers 15:24 (Abaye) and 15:26 (Rava), so the margin's citation of 15:26 is acceptable.

The mishna covers one taken out in a neck chain, one who sets sail, and one in a caravan who says 'write a get', and Passage B codifies exactly that ruling, while Passage A deals with a healthy man who kills himself.
The line quotes the phrase "זה הדבר" (Leviticus 17:2) and the Steinsaltz parenthetical cites 17:2–3 for it, so A is the verse that supplies the quoted phrase, while B lacks it.
The line states that no one permits erecting a temporary tent on Shabbat ab initio, which is the opening ruling of 315:1; 315:8 covers only the narrower case of a sloped tent.
The Semag passage states the same ruling, citing Nedarim 46: that in either case both partners are forbidden to set up a mill or oven or to raise chickens in the shared courtyard.
The line quotes I Kings 17:2 ('ויהי דבר ה' אליו לאמר') together with 17:3 ('לך מזה ופנית לך קדמה...'), so the citation to A is acceptable and B also fits.
The line quotes 'לאמר מתי יעבר החדש... להקטין איפה ולהגדיל שקל' (Amos 8:5), which is passage B; passage A (8:4) is only the verse preceding the quoted words.

The Gemara lists the signs of a saris chamah (no beard, defective hair, smooth skin, urine not foaming), which is exactly the list in SA EH 172:5; 172:6 only discusses the age at which these signs apply and the modern-day doubt about them.
Passage B states the Shabbat-eve-of-festival case where he is exempt because he could not cut on Shabbat, matching the line, while A gives only the general rule about the annulled thirty-day decree.

The line says salting meat for the pot works like the preceding case, with salt on both sides until the blood drains. A (69:4) rules on salting both sides and covers a piece salted on only one side, while B (69:3) covers only the type of salt (too fine or too coarse).
The baraita says Shabbat is mentioned in the middle of Birkat Hamazon, which 188:5 codifies as saying retzeh; 188:6 concerns forgetting, which the line does not discuss.
A restates Rav Ashi's principle that spending consecrated money as if it were non-sacred is me'ilah, while B gives the recipient's liability 'לכשיוציא', matching the gift case; A is acceptable.

The line discusses witnesses saying 'it is our handwriting but we were coerced/minors/disqualified' and the exception when others prove the handwriting, which is exactly Rambam 3:6; 3:7 covers a different case where such claims are not believed.
Both 6:15 and 6:16 state that the first consecration sanctified for its time and for the future, the principle the Gemara debates; 6:15 matches the practical ruling slightly more closely.

The baraita describes a woman who sees dam kashi (blood from hard labor) for 100 days without counting as ziva, which is the subject of Rambam 7:1 on dam kashi, while 7:8 deals with blood seen after counting seven clean days.
The parallel in Nazir is R. Yitzchak bar Yosef's statement about the agent sent to betroth a woman, which begins at the end of A and finishes in B.
The parallel is Rabba's decree in Beitzah, which begins in A ('אמר רבה: גזרה') and continues in B ('שמא יטלנו בידו ויעבירנו ארבע אמות'), split by the daf break.

The Gemara teaches that the one who blesses must taste, and Passage A rules on this: if the mekadesh did not taste but one of the diners did, the obligation is met, while the Geonim require the mekadesh to taste. Passage B deals with an interruption or a spilled cup, which this line does not discuss.
The line records Rav Dimi's ruling that the witnesses must read the get, and Rambam 1:19 codifies exactly that; 1:21 only covers the case where it was not read and she destroyed it.
The line's 'not removing her hand until she finishes' matches A's rule against leaving dough without work, while the two-vessel clause matches B, so both are drawn from it.

The line has Rava's clever-Shimon scenario (paid in land, then recovers it), which is Rambam 11:10, and it also cites Rav Naḥman's rule that a creditor reclaims land orphans collected, which is Rambam 11:9.

The Gemara rules that one who tasted food may still recite havdala (ṭaʿam mavdil), and 299:5 states exactly that; 299:6 is about a forgotten havdala and only brings the ṭaʿam rule as a secondary qualification.
The Gemara quotes 'הרי זה גיטך אם לא באתי מכאן ועד שנים עשר חדש ומת', which is the opening of Passage B, not the servant/nursing conditions of Passage A.
Rambam 8:7 codifies this exact derivation (boiling in any liquid is forbidden, from 'ובשל מבשל'), while 8:8 covers roasting/boiling combinations and anointing.
The line quotes "למען יאריכן ימיך ולמען ייטב לך", which is Deuteronomy 5:16 (B); verse 5:15 on the Exodus and Sabbath is not discussed.
The baraita quotes Numbers 6:7 and asks why it is needed given 6:6 ('על נפש מת לא יבא'), so both verses are in play and A is acceptable.
Abaye's division quotes both "ודברו" (Deut 20:5) and "ויספו" (20:8), so either verse fits and A is acceptable.
The line quotes Genesis 23:15 ('ארץ ארבע מאות שקל כסף') and then 23:16 in full, so the margin's citation of A is acceptable.

Tur OC 306 codifies this line: waiting for nightfall at the boundary for a bride or a corpse's coffin and shrouds, 'go to place X', 'if not found for a maneh, buy for two hundred', and not mentioning the price; Tur 307 does not cover this.
The quoted phrase spans Lev 17:8 ('asher ya'aleh olah o zevach') and 17:9 ('v'el petach ohel moed lo yevi'enu'), so A is acceptable.
The line quotes Genesis 13:13 and 13:14 together, so the margin's 13:14 is correct and 13:13 is also quoted.

judge.reason: The line says fruit of a planting made more than thirty days before Rosh HaShana is prohibited until 15 Shevat, as orla or revai. Rambam 9:8 codifies this: Rosh HaShana is the new year for orla and revai, the count runs from planting, and thirty days count as a year if the planting took root. Rambam 9:1 only says revai is holy and eaten in Jerusalem, which does not address the timing.
The Gemara cites the mishna that all foods and drinks may be taken for medicinal purposes on Shabbat, and Rambam 21:22 codifies this rule, including the case of drinking cress juice (ḥaltit).
The Gemara explicitly quotes Leviticus 27:26 ('אך בכור אשר יבכר לה' בבהמה... לא יקדיש איש אתו') as the source that a firstborn cannot be dedicated as another offering.

Passage A ends by quoting the opening of the same baraita/mishnah (הלוקח יין מבין הכותים), and Passage B continues with the rest of it, including R. Meir's wording; both parallel this line, so A is acceptable.

The Gemara lines quote Mishnah Keritot 3:10 (Akiva asking Eliezer about multiple Shabbat labors and the a fortiori from niddah), not 3:9, which is about slaughtering five offerings outside the Temple.
The line explicitly quotes Leviticus 1:7, 'ונתנו בני אהרן הכהן אש על המזבח', so the margin citation of A is correct; 1:6 is only the contrasting verse that Steinsaltz mentions.

ref: Mishneh Torah, Rest on a Holiday 3:16
alt: Mishneh Torah, Rest on a Holiday 3:15

judge.reason: The mishna's rule that one selects legumes in his lap, with a tray or a large vessel but not with a tablet, winnow or sieve is codified word for word in 3:15; 3:16 only covers the separate rule on when food outweighs refuse.
The line concerns emurim taken out before the sprinkling and still outside when the blood is thrown, which Passage A rules on directly; Passage B is about the meat.

Rambam 8:18 restates this Mishnah's case (cooking kodashim with chulin or kodshei kodashim with kodashim kalim, notein taam, eaten like the stricter), whereas 8:16 deals with absorption versus contact.
Passage A quotes the mishna phrase 'הזה על טהרו של מזבח', which this line explains, and Passage B discusses the same word 'טהרו' with the same 'טהר טיהרא' proverb, so both fit and A is acceptable.

The line quotes the mishna that one may borrow from and lend to gentiles and a ger toshav with interest; B states this ruling directly, while A (the rabbinic restriction on lending to gentiles, which Rav Ḥiyya's answer addresses) also fits, so A is acceptable.
The line quotes Genesis 1:2 ('והארץ היתה תהו ובהו וחשך') and then Genesis 1:3 ('ויאמר אלהים יהי אור ויהי אור'), so both verses fit and the margin's citation of A is acceptable.

ref: Mishneh Torah, Admission into the Sanctuary 1:1

judge.reason: The baraita lists both long-haired and wine-drunk priests as liable to death at Heaven's hand; A codifies the drunk priest and B the long-haired priest, so A is acceptable.
Rambam 8:4 rules on selling a slave to a gentile aside from his labor, the mitzvot, or Shabbatot and festivals, which are the cases in this line, while 8:2 covers a loan secured on the slave.
Rav Sheshet's answer that she married one of her witnesses matches Rambam 12:7 (marrying one of her witnesses, so she need not leave), which passage A lacks.
A codifies Rava's principle that consecration abrogates a lien, while B codifies the freed-slave case and the 'found in the market' rationale, so both fit this line.
The line quotes both "ויבקשו נערה יפה" (1:3) and "והנערה יפה עד מאד ותהי למלך סכנת ותשרתהו" (1:4), so A is acceptable.
B codifies the bathhouse-attendant baraita, while A codifies Rav's point that a purchase needing pulling is not meilah until pulling (for a Jew), so both are drawn from this line.
The line quotes 'one who is liable to two court-imposed death penalties is sentenced to the harsher,' which is the opening clause of Passage B; Passage A covers mixed-up offenders, a different case.

Semag 22 explicitly discusses the order of donning (arm first, then head, based on the verse) and doffing in reverse, as in this baraita, whereas B only states the basic commandment to bind on the arm.
A gives the husband's power over his wife's vows from chuppah until divorce, regardless of age, while B gives the father's power ending at bogeret; the line contrasts the two, so A is acceptable.
The line turns on "kinyan kaspo" (Lev. 22:11), which Rambam 9:7 cites, while 9:9 deals with a firstborn animal and dovecote vetches, unrelated to the line.
Passage B quotes the same verse (Lev 5:21-22) and gives the derivation of what the deposit oath excludes, while A only states the resulting ruling on land, slaves and documents.
The line directly quotes Numbers 6:7 (לאביו ולאמו לא יטמא), and the Steinsaltz and English also cite 6:6 as the general prohibition it adds to, so A is acceptable.

Passage A cites the baraita 'אין בין יום טוב לשבת אלא אוכל נפש בלבד' and discusses the laws of food preparation on Yom Tov, which is this mishna's subject, while B only prohibits work on Rosh Hashanah.
The Gemara quotes Leviticus 7:19–20 as one continuous passage; 7:19 supplies 'כל טהור יאכל בשר' and 7:20 supplies the karet clause, so A is acceptable.

ref: Mishneh Torah, Sabbatical Year and the Jubilee 9:7

judge.reason: The line's final clause 'the Sabbatical year abrogates the oath' is stated directly in Rambam 9:6, while 9:7 only limits it to oaths where an admission does not obligate payment.
Passage B has the same 'מאי בינייהו? איכא בינייהו' formula (and names Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel), while A has no such exchange and nothing about circumcision or appearance.

The Gemara says it is still forbidden to deviate in the remaining rites, like a burnt offering slaughtered not for its own sake whose blood may not be sprinkled not for its own sake; Rambam 15:3 states exactly this (one must complete the other rites lishmah, even for a meal offering whose handful was taken shelo lishmah), while 15:4 deals with a sin offering slaughtered for a different offering or for chullin.
The line's answer turns on the employer having transferred (המחהו) the wages to a storekeeper or money changer, which is exactly the exemption in B; A covers only the contractor holding the item.
Passage A discusses 'lav she'ein bo ma'aseh' and R' Yehuda's view on lashes, matching the line's key phrase, while B concerns a lav with a kum aseh.
Tur CM 200 codifies this Mishnah's law: before the measure is filled the goods are the seller's, after it is filled they are the buyer's, and a middleman whose measure breaks is liable.
The baraita says shituf of an alleyway may be made with wine or bread, matching SA 386:4 (shituf with any food); 386:6 only gives relish measures.

ref: Mishneh Torah, Foreign Worship and Customs of the Nations 9:13

judge.reason: The line gives the law of one who buys in an idolatrous market (animal's hooves cut from the knee down, produce and clothing left to rot, money and metal vessels cast into the Dead Sea), which Rambam 9:14 restates almost word for word; 9:13 concerns selling a house to idolatry.

The Steinsaltz explanation cites Leviticus 17:8–9 together; v.8 names the offering and v.9 gives the 'ונכרת' karet clause, so the citation spans both and A is acceptable.
The line quotes Proverbs 22:22 and continues into 22:23 (the 'nefesh' clause), so the citation to verse 22 is acceptable and verse 23 also fits.

The line quotes Mishnah Eruvin 10:6 verbatim (not standing in one domain and drinking in another unless head and most of body enter), while 10:4 deals with a window projection and carrying between domains.

The Gemara line is about a father who hid money and said it belongs to another or is second tithe, which is valid only if said as one relaying information and not as artifice. Passage B rules exactly that, while A concerns a deathbed bequest to Shimon and heirs who sold the estate.
The line's 'ההוא' refers to 'שובו לכם לאהליכם', which is Deuteronomy 5:27, not the 5:26 verse 'מי יתן והיה לבבם'.

The Gemara line interprets Hosea 5:2 on Jeroboam's decree against pilgrimage, while Rambam Festival Offering 1:7 deals with making up a missed festival offering after Sukkot and Shavuot, which this line does not discuss.

ref: Mishneh Torah, Offerings for Unintentional Transgressions 5:4

judge.reason: The line concerns liability for each act of bestiality, and Passage A deals with animals and per-act sin offerings, while B is about arayot generally.

The line ties the mortgaged field (mashkanta) to bar metzra law, and SA 175:57 treats the neighbor's pre-emption rights over a mortgaged field, while B (hekdesh for the poor) is unrelated.
The line quotes the Bava Batra mishna on distancing a tree (25 cubits, 50 for carob/sycamore) and which came first; B has this language, while A is about pigeons near a dovecote.
The Gemara quotes "ויחלק עליהם לילה הוא ועבדיו ויכם", which is Genesis 14:15 (Passage B); Passage A (14:14) has no part of that quotation and ends at "עד דן".

The line cites R. Yishmael's rule that a nazirite may not wash his head with clay because it makes the hair fall out, and Rambam 5:14 restates this with 'lo yachaf be'adamah'; B covers depilatory substances and does not mention clay.
The line says that by Torah law one grain exempts the whole pile (Rambam 3:1, B), and that rabbinic teruma on rabbinic-obligated produce is one-sixtieth (Rambam 3:3, A), so both passages fit.
A codifies the one-clean-day-for-one-day count of the shomeret yom keneged yom, and B defines that status for one or two days of seeing; both fit, so the cited A is acceptable.
The line quotes "וערפו העגלה" (Deut 21:4), which is the text of passage A, while passage B has only "העגלה הערופה" and does not carry the quoted phrase.
The parallel (R. Eliezer/Elazar's list plus Shmuel's explanation) is in Yevamot 84a, which A's range leads directly into and B quotes verbatim, so A is acceptable.

judge.reason: The line concerns whether matza of second tithe fulfills the obligation on Passover, and Rambam 6:8 rules on exactly this (one fulfills it with second-tithe matza in Jerusalem), while 6:1 only states the general obligation to eat matza.

judge.reason: The line concerns one versus several asham taluy offerings for repeated doubtful eating with knowledge in between, which Rambam 8:7 rules on (two offerings); 8:9 covers a different case (asham then chatat).

ref: Mishneh Torah, Those Who Defile Bed or Seat 1:8
alt: Mishneh Torah, Those Who Defile Bed or Seat 1:1

judge.reason: The line derives that menstrual blood does not make a lying or sitting item impure, only the woman does ("she, but not her blood"). ref: Mishneh Torah, Admission into the Sanctuary 4:16

judge.reason: The line says impurity is merely 'pushed aside' for the public so the tzitz is still needed, which is what Rambam 4:15 states ('דחויה היא... ומפני זה צריכה ציץ לרצות'); 4:16 does not mention the tzitz.

The line quotes Exodus 20:10 ('your manservant, your maidservant, and your cattle'), which is Passage B, while Passage A (20:9, six days you shall work) is not quoted.

The Gemara quotes "שמור את יום השבת לקדשו" (Deuteronomy 5:12), which is passage B; passage A (5:11) is about taking God's name in vain and is not quoted.
Passage A codifies the baraita's laws on greeting the rabbi and returning his greeting ("shalom alekha rabbi"), whereas B only echoes the Shechina phrase in a general statement.
The line includes רבב 'under a small cake, like a sela' (Rambam 18:10), and also הוצין, סיב and מוכין 'like a nut' (Rambam 18:12), so each passage matches part of it.
The line says hot water softens the hands and doesn't remove dirt, which Shulchan Arukh OC 181:3 repeats almost verbatim, while 181:1 only states that final waters are obligatory.

The line quotes Exodus 23:33 'lo yeshvu be'artzekha' on not letting Canaanites dwell in the land, which is the prohibition in Passage B; Passage A concerns making a covenant with the seven nations.

ref: Mishneh Torah, Rest on a Holiday 5:9

Horayot's sugya quotes this same R. Yehuda baraita on 'זאת... היא... העולה' as three exclusions; A ends with the introduction and B holds the quoted text.

judge.reason: The line's ox ready for killing and tree ready for cutting, where the defendant's claim is believed, is exactly Rambam 7:13, not 7:14 (covering blood).

Rambam 7:6 restates the line almost verbatim (fat on the masas and beit hakosot is the fat on the kerev, plus the fat on the kesalim with karet), while 7:7 covers a different point (fat inside the kesalim and kidneys).
The line likens striking (Exodus 21:15) to cursing (21:17) via the juxtaposition of the two verses, so both are discussed and A is acceptable.
The line is the dispute over whether rice is a grain for matza and chametz, which Shulchan Arukh 453:1 rules on (following the Rabbis), while 453:2 concerns a wheat-rice mixture.
The Mishnah says the bird signs were not stated in the Torah, and A (SA YD 82:1) says the same, while B gives the signs themselves, which the Mishnah only goes on to list.
The Gemara line discusses a woman who saw twelve impure days and eight remaining days of ziva, which Rambam 8:20 states almost verbatim; passage A is about presumptive kinship and is unrelated.
The line quotes Mishnah 4:3 on selling a house (door, key, mortar, itztrobil), while Passage A concerns the oil press, which is a different case.
The baraita quotes the phrase "מערב עד בקר", which appears in Exodus 27:21 (passage A), not in 27:20 (passage B).
The Gemara quotes "בם עור ופסח הרה וילדת יחדיו", which appears in passage B (31:8), not in passage A.

The Gemara discusses a monument with an added row of stones that stays forbidden even after the corpse is removed, and Shulchan Arukh YD 364:1 codifies this: a row added for the dead forbids the whole structure even after removal.
The line lists both the case of one witness saying the ketubah was paid (B) and collecting from liened property sold to buyers (A), so each ruling is drawn from it.
The Gemara quotes "הציבי לך צינים שימי לך", which appears in Jeremiah 31:21 (Passage B); Passage A (31:20) does not contain this phrase, and the Steinsaltz citation of 31:20 is off by one.
The Tur's Orach Chayim 308 passage states that raw meat, even unsalted, may be moved because it is fit for dogs, and that salted fish may be moved, which is the ruling in this baraita.

ref: Mishneh Torah, The Sanhedrin and the Penalties within Their Jurisdiction 7:8

judge.reason: The Mishna's rule that proof overturns a verdict at any time, with a 30-day window, is what Rambam 7:6 restates; 7:8 covers the separate case of a litigant who claimed to have no proof.

ref: Mishneh Torah, Second Tithes and Fourth Year's Fruit 7:9

The line deals with an agent who erred in selling, and with the objection that land has no ona'ah, which is the topic of 227:30 (agent's error, including land); 227:32 covers only land rentals.

The line has two rulings: gourds count as vegetables (the agent's question), which is A, and fresh vs. dry beans, which is B; the margin's citation of A is acceptable.

The line derives four halakhot from Hannah's verses; Tur 99 codifies the drunk-prayer ruling and Tur 101 codifies kavvanah, enunciating with the lips and not raising the voice, so both fit and A is acceptable.

ref: Mishneh Torah, Robbery and Lost Property 16:2
alt: Mishneh Torah, Robbery and Lost Property 16:3

judge.reason: The line lists coins in a pouch (Rambam 16:3) and piles of coins (Rambam 16:2), so both halachot draw on it.
The Gemara quotes "לך אמר להם שובו לכם לאהליכם", which is Deuteronomy 5:27 (passage B), while 5:26 says nothing about it.

The line states both the slave of two partners (Rambam 2:12) and the half-slave (Rambam 2:13), so each passage restates one of its rulings.

The line has two parts: comparing perforations in the lung (Rambam 7:12, 'נוקבין בה נקב אחר ומדמין'), and the rule that comparison goes only small-to-small or large-to-large (7:13), so both passages fit and A is acceptable.

The Gemara quotes only the words "ובא השמש וטהר", which appear in Leviticus 22:7 (B), not in 22:6 (A).
Passages A and B together quote the same Mishnah (wrote a get, reconsidered, townsman with same names, invalid); A has its opening and B its conclusion, so A is acceptable.
The line quotes both Numbers 15:38 (ועשו להם ציצית) and 15:39 (וראיתם אתו וזכרתם את כל מצות ה'), so the margin's A is acceptable.

The line lists several cases where a widow collects her ketubah only by oath, including one witness saying it was paid; A states the general rule that a widow collects only by oath, and B covers that specific case, so both fit.

Rambam 16:28 restates this line almost word for word (pouring from a small צלצול into a cistern, even all day, is nullified ראשון ראשון, but not from a barrel because of its significant stream), while 15:28 deals with a forbidden substance that spoils the taste of the permitted one.
The line cites the mishna to show the eating measure is wheat bread, reclining with relish, which Rambam 16:6 states; 16:7 omits the wheat measure.
The Gemara quotes "לא תעשה כל מלאכה" and the animal clause, which appear in Exodus 20:10, not in 20:9.

The Gemara line quotes the mishna on a robbed animal or slaves that aged and Rabbi Meir's dissent, which is Mishnah 9:2 (Passage B); Passage A covers wood, wool and a pregnant cow and has no aging case.
The line quotes 'Remember the Shabbat day, to keep it holy' (Exodus 20:8), which is passage B, while passage A (Exodus 20:7, the prohibition on taking God's name in vain) is not discussed.

The Gemara line says the slaughterer needs two water vessels, one for rinsing meat and one for fats, which Rambam 7:18 restates almost word for word, while 7:17 covers salting, knives and three knives.
The Mishnah line contains both the woman's seclusion ruling (A, YD 153:4) and the man's seclusion ruling (B, YD 153:2), so A is acceptable.
The line is about prayers on entering and leaving a city; A (granary measuring) and B (bathhouse) address other baraitot, though B's wording echoes the city prayer.

The Gemara line permits payment for speaking (שכר אמירה) because the Torah forbids only interest paid from borrower to lender, which is exactly what Rambam 5:14 rules; 5:16 is about renting out dinars and does not fit.
The Tur (OC 560) codifies the post-destruction ban on song at feasts, which is the same law as this mishna's statement that song was nullified from places of feasts, with the Isaiah 24:9 proof.
Passage A includes the ruling that the fat of the sciatic nerve is treated as forbidden because Israel are holy, which is the baraita quoted in the line; B is about deriving benefit.
The Gemara quotes the mishna 'על המלח ועל העצים שיהו הכהנים נאותין בהן', which appears in Passage B, while Passage A deals with gentile offerings and the High Priest's meal-offering.

ref: Mishneh Torah, Murderer and the Preservation of Life 6:8

The line quotes Rav Huna that a forced sale is valid if he says 'I want', and SA 205:1 rules that a sale under duress where the seller took payment is valid, while 205:8 covers the chamsan and the need for a protest (modea).
Passage B shares the line's 'אין גוזזין ... במספרים' ruling against shearing with scissors, while A (repairing the kondes, salting radish) has no connection.
The line quotes 'זכור את יום השבת לקדשו', which is Exodus 20:8 (passage B); passage A, Exodus 20:7, is the prohibition on taking God's name in vain and is not quoted.

The Gemara line discusses buying four or five sheep or fleeces from shepherds, with four from a small flock and five from a large one; Passage B (Theft 6:1) codifies exactly this, while Passage A gives only a general rule about whether the owner would notice.
The line quotes "כמשפט" from Leviticus 5:10 (A) and also cites "ממול ערפו" from Leviticus 5:8 (B), so A is acceptable.
The baraita has two halves: 'for a year' counts day to day (A, 220:7) and 'this year' ends at 1 Tishrei even if vowed on 29 Elul (B, 220:6), so both rulings are drawn from it.
The Gemara line lists the vitiating woman (פוגמת כתובתה), which is A, and a single witness testifying the contract was paid, which is B, so both rulings are drawn from it and A is acceptable.
The line quotes Deuteronomy 18:10 ('לא ימצא בך מעביר בנו ובתו באש...') and continues into vv. 11-12; verse 9 is not quoted, so B is the cited verse.

The Gemara quotes 'שחט ישראל וקבל הכהן, נתנו לחבירו, וחברו לחבירו', which is the text of Mishnah 5:6 (Passage B), while Passage A only describes the three groups and the rows of priests holding basins.

Passage A discusses the Gemara's rule that collection is from real estate and not movables, and the Geonic enactment that departs from it; B only covers the later custom of writing movables into the ketubah.
Rambam 5:14 restates Rava's two rulings (giving a dinar so someone lends to another, and paying for the act of asking), while 5:16 only prohibits renting out dinars.

The Gemara line is about a bird sitting between two tree branches, and Rambam 13:16 codifies it almost verbatim: if the branches were removed and she would fall on the nest, one must send her away. Passage B concerns a bird sitting among the eggs without touching them, which is a different case.

The Gemara line says remnants of cloaks under three by three fingerbreadths may not be moved because they suit neither poor nor rich, which Rambam 26:6 restates almost word for word; 26:8 covers doors and mats, which this line does not discuss.

The Gemara line teaches that reciting Shema with precise enunciation cools Gehenna, and Tur OC 62 quotes this exact statement of Rav Chama bar Chanina, while Tur OC 60 only discusses the blessings and kavana.
Rav Kahana says a lung that looks like flesh is a tereifa, and Shulchan Arukh YD 38:1 rules that a lung resembling the color of flesh is tereifa, while 35:1 covers perforated lungs.
Passage A's ruling on vessels pushed into a pit (man and ox owner liable, pit owner exempt) restates this line, while B addresses a pushed pregnant woman.

Passage A rules that even a gentile who speaks offhandedly is believed for a woman's husband's death, which is Rav Ashi's point that offhand speech is valid only for a woman's testimony; B covers the same ground but is less direct.

ref: Mishneh Torah, Admission into the Sanctuary 4:12

judge.reason: The Rambam passage says Passover-offering-type communal sacrifices override only corpse impurity, and that those impure from a creeping animal may not be involved. That is related to the line's topic, but the line concerns slaughtering and sprinkling the individual Paschal lamb for someone impure from a creeping animal (Ulla's dispute), which the Rambam would codify in Korban Pesach.
Semag negative 87 sits in the section on the slanderer/motzi shem ra, but the cited text is only a pointer to the next commandment, so it doesn't clearly state this ruling.
The line opens with rinsing and washing the cup of blessing, which is exactly SA 183:1, while 183:3 (a whole cup) is not among the ten items.

Passage B's 'reishit ono' principle (firstborn for inheritance only if no earlier live child) matches the line's point that this child is not an inheritance-firstborn, while A concerns a mix-up of two sons.

Passage B cites Ketubot 48 and the derivation that a father who delivers his daughter to the husband's messengers makes her liable to strangulation; Passage A concerns bestiality and does not touch this line.

The line discusses 'ביתו ריקם מן העבירה' and 'פרקו נאה' (no bad reputation in youth), which Rambam 4:4 codifies ('ביתו ריקן מן העברות', 'לא יצא עליו שם רע בילדותו'), while 4:3 only says a fitting prayer leader is appointed.

The Mishnah gives minimum sizes for dividing a courtyard (4 cubits), field (9 kav) and garden (half kav), which is exactly Rambam Neighbors 1:4; 1:5 covers other items (hall, dovecote, bathhouse, garment) that this line does not mention.
The baraita says outside-matter intention is piggul and inside-matter intention is not; B states both halves and A gives the inside-matter example (sprinkling), so A is an acceptable citation.
The line expounds 'חומה' (Lev 25:30, passage A) and 'סביב' (Lev 25:31, passage B), so it draws on both verses and A is acceptable.
Passage A ends by quoting the same Mishnah (כתב לגרש את אשתו ונמלך...), and Passage B just continues that same sentence, so the margin's citation to A fits.

Rambam Theft 1:14 covers the same topic of valuation at theft versus at judgment, but it rules on the double payment and is silent on Rabba's view that a thief who breaks or drinks the wine pays the principal at the higher value.
The line quotes Deut 3:4 ("sixty cities, all the region of Argov") and Deut 3:5 ("all these cities were fortified with high walls"), so A is acceptable and B also fits.

judge.reason: The Gemara permits relying on a gentile's advice that one potion is good and another harmful, which matches Rambam 12:10 (one may ask a gentile doctor, but not take from him), while 12:9 deals with taking treatment from gentiles.
The line quotes Leviticus 5:8 ('והקריב את אשר לחטאת ראשונה') and also Leviticus 5:10 ('ואת השני יעשה עולה כמשפט'), so the margin's citation of 5:10 is valid.
The Mishnah's perforated gullet, brain membrane and heart to its chamber are exactly the organs in Rambam 6:1, while 7:1 concerns lung membranes.
The Gemara derives from 'אשר יזה מדמה' that blood already sprinkled does not require laundering, which is the case in A (spattering from the remainder after the four placements).
The line quotes 'לא תעשון כן לה' אלהיכם', which is the text of Deuteronomy 12:4 (passage A); verse 12:3 is only the surrounding context.

The line quotes II Sam 16:3 (Ziba's slander) and 16:4 (David's acceptance), so the margin's 16:2 does not match exactly, but the cited chapter and the nearby verse 16:4 both fit; the reference is plausibly off by one or two.

The line includes trenches and water channels (חריצין ונעיצין) as forbidden and excludes pits, ditches and caves as permitted; A rules on the trenches and channels, B on the pits, ditches and caves, so each draws on half of it.

ref: Mishneh Torah, Rest on a Holiday 6:13
alt: Mishneh Torah, Rest on a Holiday 7:13

judge.reason: The line forbids writing Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot on Chol HaMoed and allows Rabbi Yehuda's personal-use case, which Rambam 7:13 restates; Passage A (6:13) is about eruv tavshilin and terumah on Rosh Hashanah and has nothing to do with it.
The line quotes "לא ידבק בידך מאומה מן החרם" to forbid deriving benefit from an idol ground into fertilizer, which is exactly Passage B's prohibition; Passage A concerns making decorative images.

The line is the gezerah shava 'מעיני' between idol worship and communal sin-offering, which is the same derivation as in B ('נאמר כאן מעיני ונאמר להלן מעיני'), while A is a different gezerah shava on 'קהל'.
A codifies the court-agent seizure and the 'two utensils, take one and return one' ruling, while B cites the Deut 24:10 ban on entering the house; A is acceptable.

The line states both that a condition of no blemishes voids the betrothal and that all blemishes disqualifying priests disqualify women; SA 39:3 codifies the first and SA 39:4 the second, so A is acceptable.

The Gemara line is the Mishnah itself, and Passage B (Bava Batra 5:1) contains this exact text (wagon/mules, yoke/oxen, Rabbi Yehuda on the price), while Passage A (5:3) covers a donkey's foal, a dunghill, a pit and a beehive, which this line does not discuss.
The Mishnah states both rules: A codifies the small-to-large and one-to-two prohibitions, and B codifies the opposite-opening ban and the public-domain permission.
The line deals with fringes attached without first cutting the strand ends being unfit, which is what SA 11:13 rules; 11:12 only covers the number of strands.
The line quotes 'אנא ה' הצליחה נא' (Ps 118:25) and 'ברוך הבא בשם ה'' (Ps 118:26), so both verses fit and the margin's citation of 118:26 is acceptable.
The line quotes Exodus 15:23 ("ויבואו מרתה ולא יכלו לשתות") and then 15:24 ("וילן העם על משה"), so the margin's citation of 15:24 is acceptable.
A rules the earth-intervening-between-rock-and-border case a doubt (Rav Pappa), while B rules the earth-above/rock-below case a doubt (Rav Ashi); both dilemmas appear in this line.
The Gemara line is about the blessing 'Who knows all secrets' on seeing a multitude of Israel, which Rambam Blessings 10:11 codifies, while 6:11 is about washing hands and is unrelated.
The line concerns Rava's ruling that 'take your get from the ground' is not a valid giving, whereas A covers invalid witnesses and B covers a get given with an exclusion condition.

The Gemara line is R. Meir's homily on Ecclesiastes 7:2 about taking death to heart, while Rambam Marriage 13:11 covers a husband's duty to give his wife a cloak for going out and his right to limit her outings, which only mentions a house of mourning in passing.

The cited passage from Sefer Mitzvot Gadol quotes Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua's ruling from Shevuot 42a: if the creditor is deemed credible 'like three' and the debtor repays before four, the debt is considered paid. That is exactly the content of this line.
The Gemara quotes 'ואף הסיתך מפי צר רחב לא מוצק תחתיה', which is Job 36:16 (B), while verse 15 is not quoted in the Gemara's own text.
The Gemara quotes "זה הדבר אשר צוה ה' לבנות צלפחד", which is the opening of Numbers 36:6 (passage B); passage A (36:5) does not contain this text.

The Gemara line on seeking water up to a parasang ahead, and less than a mil behind, is codified almost word for word in SA OC 92:4, while 92:6 deals with cleaning a soiled place with earth or stones and does not fit.

Passage A ends by quoting the same baraita, 'אחרים אומרים: יכול יהא בכור שעיברה שנתו', and Passage B continues it with the same derivation from the second tithe, so together they parallel both lines of the Gemara and A is acceptable.

The baraita covers a competent Israelite woman betrothed to a competent priest who then became deaf-mute, and then the case of the deaf-mute yavam. Rambam 8:10 codifies exactly this, while 8:9 deals with a deaf-mute husband in marriage.

The Gemara line covers the eighth day falling on Shabbat before a Festival, which permits a haircut on Friday; Rambam 10:7 restates this (the 'anus' rationale), while 10:6 addresses the sixth day, where no haircut is allowed.

The baraita says one who betrothes a woman collects 200 for a virgin or 100 for a widow, which matches SA EH 55:6 on a betrothed woman collecting her ketubah when he dies or divorces her; 55:7 concerns the father's rights to his daughter's ketubah.
The line turns on the verse 'ויראת מאלהיך' about verbal mistreatment, which Rambam 14:12 quotes, while 14:13 only gives later examples of verbal wronging.

The Tur (EH 15) codifies the baraita's law that a son's wife is forbidden by Torah law and the wives of his son's son and later descendants are forbidden by rabbinic law "until the end of all generations"; it also mentions the daughter's-line variants.
The baraita covers both the large/small candelabrum (B, 88:25) and the large/small belt (A, 88:26), so both rulings derive from this line and the margin's A is acceptable.
Passage A is only a pointer ('see mitzvah 144') to the chadash text in B, which states R. Yochanan ben Zakkai's rule that the whole day of waving is prohibited.
The line excludes chalut (boiled matza), which 454:3 addresses, and also covers ashisha and fine flour, which 454:1 addresses, so both rulings come from it.
The line has an egg clause (A: egg needs 60 besides itself) and an udder clause counted in the 60 (B: כחל מן המנין), so both rulings come from it.

judge.reason: The line recounts the Greek defilement and Hasmonean victory (Rambam 3:1) and also the single cruse lasting eight days (3:2).
The Gemara explicitly quotes "מבשרו" from Leviticus 15:2 ("כי יהיה זב מבשרו") to show that a discharge caused by circumstances beyond his control does not make him a zav.
The line's poor person/homeowner carrying out and bringing in is the hand-to-hand scenario Tur 347 rules on, while Tur 346 is only a general statement of the domains.
The line discusses whether a ship is acquired by passing (mesira), which is what Passage B rules; Passage A is about acquiring the rental of movable objects with money and does not concern this line.
The Gemara line quotes the mishna 'שבועה שלא אוכל ככר זו... אינו חייב אלא אחת', which is Mishnah 3:7 (B); Mishnah 3:8 (A) covers shav'ah oaths and does not contain this passage.

The line discusses the verse 'לנכרי תשיך' and whether it permits or commands taking interest from a gentile, which is exactly what Rambam 5:1 quotes and rules, while 5:2 deals with rabbinic restrictions on lending to gentiles.

judge.reason: The line derives the ten-person requirement for devarim shebikdusha from Leviticus 22:32; Passage B quotes that verse and states the rule, while Passage A states the same requirement for kedusha, Torah reading and haftarah, so A is acceptable.

The line quotes R. Akiva's principle that any labor doable before Shabbat does not override it; A applies it to preparations for circumcision (the knife), and B states the same principle explicitly ("זה הכלל"), so both fit and A is acceptable.
The line has Yehoshua ben Gamla instituting teachers in every province and town (Passage B) and admitting children at age six or seven (Passage A), so both rulings come from it and A is acceptable.
The quoted words 'ביום זבחכם יאכל וממחרת והנותר עד יום' appear in Leviticus 19:6, while 19:5 only has the introductory 'וכי תזבחו זבח שלמים', which the Steinsaltz adds as context.

The line contains both the mishna's rule against protesting poor gentiles taking gleanings (Passage B) and the baraita on sustaining, visiting and burying gentiles for the ways of peace (Passage A), so the margin's citation of A is acceptable.
The line cites Zelek the Ammonite (II Sam 23:37, passage A) and then Uriah the Hittite (23:39, passage B), so both verses are quoted and A is acceptable.

The line quotes R. Eliezer ben Ya'akov's baraita that a large animal that expels a mass of blood is exempt from the firstborn law and the mass is buried, which is exactly Rambam 4:11; 4:12 covers fetal development and the animal's conception interval, which this line does not discuss.
The line distinguishes a field near a marsh from one not near a marsh, which is the subject of SA 576:6; 576:7 deals with houses in desolate places and a beast taking a child.

The line's exception for overabundant rain and R. Yohanan's reason ('one does not pray over an excess of good') appear in Tur 577, while Tur 576 only lists the troubles for which they fast and sound the alarm.

judge.reason: The line concerns women, slaves and minors being believed when they say they searched a house presumed unsearched, which is codified in B (2:17), while A deals with who must search between landlord and tenant.
The line concerns schoolchildren reading by candlelight because of their teacher's fear, which is exactly the ruling in OC 275:6, not the Bameh Madlikin reading in 275:7.

The Mishna's closing clause ("I specified but forgot" or "my father told me" means the largest is consecrated) matches Rambam 16:9, which restates it; 16:8 covers the earlier clauses and rules differently for three animals (largest, with concern for the middle one).
The line covers Nasi/Av Beit Din/Chakham (B, 244:15) and also sons of sages stepping over heads and returning after leaving (A, 244:16), so A is acceptable.
The line teaches both not burying weights in salt (A, 231:11) and not measuring land differently in summer and winter (B, 231:18), so A is acceptable.
Rambam 1:21 codifies the mishna's lost/burned eiruv invalid before dark for chatzerot, but not Rava's four-cubit rule on an eiruv rolling beyond the techum.
A matches the 'even niddah, even ill' clause of the line, while B matches the earlier clause on four weeks of announcements and the 'lose even a hundred maneh' warning.

The Gemara line discusses the order of the havdala blessings (wine, spices, light), which is the order SA OC 296:1 sets with the mnemonic יבנ"ה; 297:1 deals only with whether to recite the spices blessing.
The line quotes "היום על לבבך", which is found in Deuteronomy 6:6 and not in 6:5, which has "בכל לבבך" but no "היום".
The line concerns wine carried by a gentile and sealed with only one seal, and Shulchan Arukh YD 118:1 codifies the two-seal requirement along with the view that one seal suffices in certain cases.

The line is the mishnah itself, and Passage A (4:5) repeats its formula 'מפני תקון העולם כופין את רבו ועושה אותו בן חורין וכותב שטר על דמיו', so it is a valid parallel, though B is the exact same text.
The line discusses a notch with an edge on one side versus two sides, which matches Rambam 1:15 on a one-sided groove, whereas 1:17 covers knives with no notch.

Tur 386 includes the parenthetical ruling that a homeowner in partnership with his neighbors, one in wine and one in oil, need not establish a shittuf, which restates this mishna; Tur 387 covers relying on an eiruv in place of a shittuf, which is a different topic.
The line quotes 'לך אמר להם שובו לכם לאהליכם', which is Deuteronomy 5:27 (Passage B), not the 'מי יתן' text of verse 26.
The Tur (YD 292) codifies the mishnah Abaye cites (a non-kosher bird on kosher eggs, or the reverse, is exempt) and the qore-female exception that this line discusses.

The line lists several conditions for me'ilah: damage and benefit together, from the same item, and the agent who fulfilled his agency. Passage B (Trespass 6:1) codifies the first conditions and A (Trespass 7:1) codifies the agent condition, so A is acceptable.

judge.reason: Rambam 14:6 restates Rava's ruling: taking a coin before despair violates a positive commandment and two prohibitions, and returning it after despair is only a gift, so the transgression stands. Passage B covers different cases: intent to return at first, and taking only after despair.

The line derives that the burnt-offering bird's head is fully separated when pinched, which is codified in 6:20 ('מולק ומבדיל, ואם לא הבדיל פסולה'), not in 6:21's handling of the head and body afterward.
The line quotes 'והדוד האחד תאנים רעות מאד אשר לא תאכלנה מרע', which appears in Jeremiah 24:2 (Passage B), while 24:1 only mentions the two baskets of figs.
The line is a verbatim quote of Mishnah Nedarim 8:3 (harvest, grape harvest, olive harvest and the general principle), while 8:2 deals only with Pesach.
The line explains the mishna on a cow sent via the lender's slave (Hebrew slave per Shmuel), which A codifies explicitly; B's stick case appears only as Rav's analogy.
The line quotes 'ish tzaru'a hu' (13:44) as the verse under discussion and 'vehatzaru'a asher bo hanega' (13:45) as the source of the derivation, so A is acceptable.
The line quotes Hosea 1:2 ('לך קח לך אשת זנונים וילדי זנונים') and then Hosea 1:3 ('וילך ויקח את גמר בת דבלים'), so the margin's citation of A is acceptable.
The line quotes the baraita on not decreeing fasts on Rosh Chodesh, Hanukkah and Purim, which Rambam Fasts 1:7 codifies; 1:6 covers Shabbat and festivals, not discussed here.
The Mishnah's opening clause (animals and vessels follow the owner's feet) matches A, and its son/shepherd clause matches B, so A is acceptable.

The line says the veins in the jaw are forbidden, and Shulchan Arukh YD 65:1 lists the veins of the lower jaw among those forbidden because of blood, while 65:3 deals with the wing and jaw bone of fowl.

judge.reason: The mishna's phrase 'what he did is done, and he pays from his home' appears nearly verbatim in Rambam 6:3, while 6:4 covers an unqualified, unaccepted judge.
Rambam 8:2 says that if the seller was not demanding, the buyer acquires the whole field and the remainder is an ordinary debt, matching the line's written-debt solution.
Passage A repeats the R. Elazar b. Yosei baraita on 'asher lo chomah' verbatim, while B also has the 'two tannaim / alternatively R. Elazar b. Yosei said it' framing, so both are valid parallels.

judge.reason: The line opens by quoting the mishna on a few presents used in her father's house (A), then gives Ravin's rule on presents returning except food and drink (B).

The line closes the chapter on covering the blood, and A (kisui hadam for a fetus) belongs to that chapter, while B (gid hanasheh) belongs to the next chapter.
The Gemara quotes 'אם לא יגאל השדה... והיה השדה בצאתו ביובל', which spans Leviticus 27:20 (opening) and 27:21 (the Jubilee clause), so citing A is acceptable.

The line is about a receipt found among the debtor's documents for the note of Yosef ben Shimon, with two men of that name, and Rambam 24:8 codifies this almost word for word, while 24:1 only covers writing documents when the other party is absent.
Ameimar's ruling has two halves: A codifies the 'al da'at rabbim' half (no annulment), B codifies the 'berabbim' half (annulment possible).

ref: Mishneh Torah, Foreign Worship and Customs of the Nations 9:15

judge.reason: The Gemara line on buying in an idolatrous market (animal hamstrung, produce rots, money cast into the Dead Sea) is restated in Rambam 9:14, while 9:15 covers an idolater's wedding feast.
The Gemara quotes Hosea 10:4-5 as one span, starting with 'דברו' (verse 4) and continuing through 'על כבודו כי גלה ממנו' (verse 5), so the cited verse A is acceptable.
The line quotes the Shammai/Hillel/Sages dispute on ḥalla measures, which is nearly verbatim Eduyot 1:2, while Eduyot 1:3 concerns drawn water in a mikveh.
The Gemara line is about the roof of the crop (גגו של זפק) being treated like the gullet, which is exactly what Rambam 6:17 rules; 6:15 deals with intestines that came out or were overturned.
Passage A parallels Rav Shimi bar Hiyya's derivation from 'ככל אשר אני מראה אותך' in line 4, and B parallels the Rava objection and answers in lines 5-7, so A fits and B also fits.
The line quotes Job 14:9 (B) verbatim, but Steinsaltz cites the quotation as Job 14:8-9, so A is the opening verse of the same passage.

Rambam Marriage 7:13 rules on a betrothal made with the exception 'except for so-and-so' (she is forbidden to everyone but him) and holds it is doubtful betrothal, which is the case Rabbi Abba's dilemma raises in Gittin 82b.
The line uses the same 'מעכבין זה את זה' formula as the Mishnah list in A, while B concerns gold as the material, not mutual prevention.
The line quotes Psalms 37:32 ('The wicked watches the righteous') and then 37:33 ('The Lord will not leave him in his hand'), so the margin's citation of 37:33 is valid.

The Gemara line discusses assessing the udder (kahal) in its own volume for the milk it releases into a pot, while Rambam 9:18 covers salted food that is inedible because of its salt being treated like hot food, which is a different topic.

Rambam 29:22 gives Rava's order for a festival on motzei Shabbat (wine, kiddush, candle, havdala, shehecheyanu), matching the Gemara's ruling, while B covers ordinary motzei Shabbat without kiddush or zeman.
The Mishnah is about a potter bringing pots into a courtyard, which Rambam 3:13 restates almost word for word; 3:14 is about produce and the oven story, so the margin's A is an off-by-one error.
The line quotes Hosea 1:3-9, beginning with 'ותהר ותלד לו בן' (A) and continuing with the Jezreel verse (B), so A is acceptable.

The line derives from 'lo tasim damim' that one may not keep a dangerous item such as a vicious dog or unsteady ladder, and 427:8 rules on removing hazards and cites 'lo tasim damim', whereas 427:6 concerns only a roof without a parapet.
The line quotes Leviticus 25:28 for the ancestral field and Leviticus 25:30 for the walled-city houses, so the cited verse 25:30 is acceptable.

The mishna says the three cities across the Jordan do not admit killers until all six are designated, and Passage B states this ('אין אחת קולטת עד שיבדלו כולם', citing Makkot 9b), while Passage A deals with who is exiled and the rules of return.
The line asks about the מרדעת, which is in A (9:5), and quotes R. Yosei's builders/ignoramus ruling, which is in B (9:6); A is acceptable.

The line is the Mishnah on selling a house (door, key, mortar, itztrobil, 'he and all that is in it'), which is word-for-word Mishnah Bava Batra 4:3 (B), while A covers selling a courtyard.
The Eruvin line quotes the Shabbat baraita about turnips buried under a vine, which spans A (the opening, 'מקצת עליו מגולים אינו חושש') and B (the list of concerns and 'ניטלין בשבת').

The Gemara cites the baraita about clothing of the poor, and Rambam 22:20 addresses the poor person's garment and 'other clothing of the poor', while 22:21 concerns scraps under three by three.

The line distinguishes anumlin (wine, honey, pepper), which is permitted on Shabbat, from aluntit (wine, water, balsam), which is forbidden, and Rambam 22:11 restates exactly this, while 22:12 covers mustard, garlic and similar preparations.

The line is Rabban Gamliel's pre-paid and late interest, and Rambam 5:11 restates it nearly word for word, while 5:13 covers asking the borrower to host a guest, which is a different matter.

The line permits removing a container of excrement or urine to the garbage heap (A, 308:34) and requires adding water before returning it (B, 308:35), so both rulings come from it and A is acceptable.

The line discusses selling a daughter to relatives, which Rambam 4:11 codifies, and also the widow to a High Priest and divorcée or ḥalutza to a common priest, which Rambam 4:12 codifies, so A is acceptable.

The line has two rulings: a doubtful egg is prohibited, which is A (513:2), and an egg mixed into a thousand eggs makes them all prohibited, which is B (513:1); A is acceptable.

The Mishnah enumerates the seven substances, and Rambam 9:37 lists those same seven substances, while 9:36 only states the general rule.

The line requires an oath and caps recovery at the enhancement value; 375:8 states the oath requirement for appraised claims, while 375:7 does not address the oath.

The line asks whether the court removes a garment one party seized in its presence, which is what Rambam 9:12 rules on; 9:11 only covers holding the whole garment versus hanging on.
The line's twelve-day limit is explained by twilight birth on Shabbat eve and the two days of Rosh Hashana, which Passage B rules on, while Passage A covers an eighth-month birth.
The quoted line spans Lev 27:20 (ואם לא יגאל... ואם מכר את השדה) and 27:21 (והיה השדה בצאתו ביובל), so A is acceptable.

The line is the mishna on windows (four cubits above, below, opposite) with the baraita's reasons; Rambam 7:2 codifies the four-cubit distance and height to prevent peering, while 7:4 deals with a different case of a wall beside the window at one handbreadth.

ref: Mishneh Torah, Shofar, Sukkah and Lulav 6:6

The line is about a person's four cubits acquiring ownerless items, while the cited Semag passage covers honest weights and measures (Bava Batra 88-89), so there is no connection.

The line quotes Esther 2:15 (ותהי אסתר נשאת חן) and also Esther 2:16 (ותלקח אסתר... חדש טבת), so the margin's citation of A is acceptable.

judge.reason: The Mishnah's rulings on the kasva thief, cursing by a sorcerer, the Aramean woman and the impure priest are restated in Rambam 18:6, while 11:6 only covers the order of judges' opinions.

The line says the watchman need not sit and guard constantly and may go in and out; A (13:3) rules the wine permitted though the watchman enters and exits, and B (13:4) states that the watchman need not sit and guard constantly.
The line quotes "צמר ופשתים" (Deut 22:11) and the following tzitzit commandment "גדילים תעשה לך" (Deut 22:12), so the citation spans both verses and A is acceptable.
Both Arakhin passages contain Rabbi Elazar bar Yosei's baraita on 'אשר לוא חומה'; B also repeats the 'איבעית אימא' formula, but A is acceptable.

judge.reason: Both Rambam passages codify Rabba's rule that showing voluntarily makes one liable; A gives the voluntary-informer case, B states the voluntary versus coerced distinction.
A restates the closing clause (all priestly blemishes disqualify women), while B codifies the stipulation of 'no blemishes'; both are drawn from this line, so A is acceptable.

The Ketubot line is a parallel of Yevamot 88a-b, where "סוף סוף תרי ותרי נינהו" at the end of A introduces B's "באשם תלוי קאי... כגון שניסת לאחד מעדיה", so A, which the margin cites, contains the opening of the parallel and B contains the rest.

The Mishna covers the whole procedure, and both Rambam passages restate parts of it: A has taking the head, the salt and the throwing onto the fire, B has ascending the ramp, pinching and squeezing the blood; the margin's A is acceptable.
The line quotes "ושורך וחמרך וכל בהמתך", which is in Deuteronomy 5:14 (B), not in 5:13 (A).
The line names the camel driver's and sailor's knots, which Rambam 10:1 gives as examples of liable knots, while 10:2 covers exempt ordinary knots.

The line is about a woman who says she is married and then says she is unmarried, and is believed only if she gives an amatla. This is exactly Shulchan Arukh EH 47:4, while 46:4 deals with a public rumor of betrothal and an amatla offered against that rumor.
The Gemara quotes Jeremiah 52:6 (ninth of the month, famine) and then 52:7 (ותבקע העיר), so the margin citing 52:7 fits and 52:6 is also quoted.
Passage B explicitly discusses a poor person valuating a rich one giving the poor valuation, while A covers age and gender cases, not means.
The Gemara line is about one who betroths his sister (Rav: money returned; Shmuel: gift), which SA EH 50:2 rules on directly, while 50:1 covers general cases of when betrothal money is returned.
The line cites Numbers 6:19 on the nazirite's ram (the cooked foreleg), and Rambam 9:9 codifies exactly that case, while 9:11 only covers ordinary shelamim and the chest and thigh.
Tur OC 688 includes the ruling that when Purim falls on Shabbat the Megillah is not read on Shabbat but is read early, on Friday, which is the law this Gemara line explains with Rabba's decree.

The line says one without water wipes his hands with earth, a stone or a splinter; A (92:6) allows cleaning with earth or stones, and B (92:4) allows wiping with a stone or earth when there is no water, so both fit and A is acceptable.
The line says a mourner counts toward the three for zimun in Grace after Meals, which is what SA YD 379:5 rules; 379:3 is about a different blessing wording.
The line concerns the thirty-day ban on ironed garments and the dispute over new or white garments, which SA 389:5 codifies (ironed, white and new), while 389:3 deals with the seven days.
