judge.reason: The line gives the meat-fish-wine-oil chain (Rambam 6:7's examples) and ends with 'the last is caught, the produce itself remains' (the principle in 6:6), so A is acceptable.
The baraita's rule that separate drops (טפין טפין) do not combine is exactly the ruling in 190:8, whereas 190:5 only gives the general bean-plus-bit threshold.
The line turns on the mishna that a dead firstborn donkey must be buried because benefit is prohibited, which Passage A states directly ("ואם מת... יקבר מפני שהוא אסור בהנאה").

The line quotes Rava's statement not to sit at the mouth of the side post, which appears in Shabbat 141a (A) and, together with the women with jugs challenge, in Shabbat 148b (B); both fit, and A is acceptable.
The line is about forbidden and permitted calculations on Shabbat, including past ones, which SA 307:6 codifies, while 307:7 deals with saying a worker should be ready for the evening.

The Gemara quotes Leviticus 22:13 "ובת כהן כי תהיה אלמנה וגרושה" to exclude a gentile or slave, and Passage B quotes exactly that verse, while Passage A deals with a different verse (22:12) and a different law.
The Gemara line says that witnesses are liable for an oath outside court only if they deny in court, and Rambam 9:2 codifies exactly this, while B concerns witnesses to a fine, which is unrelated.

The Mishnah line lists honey among the permitted foods (A: honey of a gentile is permitted) and also grape clusters, pickles, tarit, brine and ḥiltit (B), so both rulings derive from it, and A is acceptable.
The line concerns a craftsman holding the owner's cloak and whether the owner saw it in his hand, which is the subject of 89:5, not the general hired-worker price dispute in 89:4.
Tur EH 66 states the 200/100 amounts and that the husband may add to the ketubah, matching the Mishnah's opening; EH 67 covers other cases without the addition.
The line states that a virgin who is a widow, divorcée or ḥalutza from nisuin gets a ketubah of 100, and Rambam 11:1 states exactly this ruling; 11:2 only gives the reason.
Rambam 12:5 restates this line's rulings (killing after he separated is punishable; the transgressor who kills the zealot in self-defense is exempt), while 12:8 is unrelated.
The line lists small intestines perforated (A, 6:13) and also the rumen and omasum/reticulum perforated outward (B, 6:11), so both rulings derive from it.
The Gemara quotes Psalms 107:17-21 in sequence, including both 'ישלח דברו וירפאם' (v.20) and 'יודו לה' חסדו' (v.21), so the margin's citation of v.21 is acceptable.

The Tur rules that when a field is sold to a gentile, we excommunicate the seller until he accepts liability for all harm that comes from the gentile ("משמתינן ליה... כל אונסא"), which restates this Gemara line almost word for word.
The line's 'מלא תרוד רקב שנתפזר בבית... ורבי שמעון מטהר' is nearly verbatim Mishnah Oholot 3:2 (Passage B), while Passage A deals with divided items and R. Dosa.

The line is about a perforated rectum (חלחולת) being kosher in the place where it is attached to the hips, which Rambam 6:16 codifies; 6:15 covers intestines that protrude or turn over and does not mention the rectum.
Rambam 12:11 restates this line's rulings on the bier (matzhivin) and on being known to the public (mitasekin), while 12:10 covers infant burial by age.
The line concludes that an animal lacking upper teeth is kosher, which is the practical rule in Rambam 1:3 (check for no upper teeth, provided it is not a camel).

The Gemara line is about an oven that was fired and swept, where roasting the Paschal lamb is not 'roasted in fire', and Rambam 8:10 codifies exactly this (הסיק את התנור וגרף... אין זה צלי אש), while B covers raw/partly roasted meat.

The Gemara line is about exchanging a donkey for a cow and a lamb where only the cow was pulled, which is exactly the case in Passage B (203:2: no acquisition, no complete pulling), whereas Passage A states the general rule of exchange.
The Gemara quotes Zephaniah 3:6 ('הכרתי גוים') and then 3:7 ('אמרתי אך תיראי אותי'), so the line spans both verses and the margin's citation of 3:7 is acceptable.
The line quotes both Psalms 102:1 ("תפלה לעני כי יעטף") and Psalms 120:1 ("אל ה' בצרתה לי קראתי"), so the margin's citation of Psalms 102:1 is valid.
The line discusses the omitted 'in between' (בין הביניים) of the grape, which Steinsaltz and the English tie to the verse 'מחרצנים ועד זג' (Numbers 6:4), the verse the cited passage contains.

The line distinguishes eating less than satiety (rabbinic obligation, so a minor can fulfill it for his father) from eating to satiety (Torah obligation), which is exactly Rambam 5:16; 5:15 only states that a son may bless for his father, without this distinction.
The line has two rulings: no kneading in the sun or with sun-heated water (SA 459:1), and the need for two vessels, one for mixing and one for cooling hands (SA 459:3); A is acceptable.
Passage A explicitly rules it is permitted to insulate cold food on Shabbat, which is Shmuel's statement in this line; B deals with transferring hot food to another vessel.
The line ends by introducing the mishna in Demai 7:4 (R. Yehuda denies bererah), and the Meilah passage quotes that same mishna, 'הלוקח יין מבין הכותים', which is the parallel.
The baraita quotes "דבר אל בני ישראל" from Lev 1:2 and "וסמך" from Lev 1:4, so both verses are cited and A is acceptable.

The line quotes the baraita that an alleyway is permitted by a side post or beam only if houses and courtyards open into it, and Passage A codifies exactly this ('אין מבוי ניתר בלחי או קורה עד שיהיו פתוחים לתוכו שני חצרות'), while Passage B covers a courtyard that is longer than it is wide.
The line quotes the mishnah about a grown woman waiting twelve months and Rabbi Eliezer's 'since her husband is obligated for her sustenance, he may annul', which appears in Passage B and not in A.
The quoted words 'וזרעתי את בית ישראל ... זרע אדם וזרע בהמה' appear in Passage B (31:27), not in A, which is 'על זאת הקיצתי'.
The Mishnah's ruling that slaughter from the sides is valid (and from the nape is a problem) is what SA YD 20:3 codifies, while 20:1 only defines the slaughter location by the cap and the windpipe.
The Gemara line rules on bathing the whole body, the face, hands and feet, and smearing with oil, which Tur YD 381 states almost verbatim; Tur 380 covers mourner's work prohibitions.
The line quotes 'הוצאתיה נאם ה' צבאות ובאה אל בית הגנב...' which is verbatim Zechariah 5:4 (Passage B), while Passage A (5:3) is only mentioned in the English context.
The line concludes a woman may be an agent for delivery, which matches Rambam 6:6 on who is qualified as agent for delivery (excluding only the five); 6:10 is about changing an agent's role.
The quoted words 'בבקר בבקר בהיטיבו את הנרות ... יקטירנה' appear in Exodus 30:7, not 30:8, which speaks of the evening lighting.

The line has two rulings: shehakol over meat, milk, eggs and cheese (Rambam 8:1), and shehakol over moldy bread, soured wine, spoiled dishes, salt, truffles and mushrooms (Rambam 8:8), so A is acceptable.

The line's wording (eaten within the curtains by male priests, in any manner of food, a day and a night until midnight) matches Mishnah 5:5 on communal peace offerings and guilt offerings, while 5:4 covers the burnt offering, which is not eaten.

The line lists that a betrothed man does not mourn or become impure for his betrothed, does not inherit her, and that she collects her ketubah if he dies; B codifies the first points and A codifies the ketubah point, so A is acceptable.

Passage B (Positive Commandments 106) discusses Sanhedrin 6 directly: the mitzvah of mediation (bitzua) and the verse 'mishpat veshalom shifetu b'sha'arekhem', 'which judgment has peace, this is bitzua'. Passage A's visible text covers other laws and never reaches this ruling.

The line opens with one who carries produce from place to place and a friend asking for it now in exchange for produce at the destination, permitted only if he has produce there. Rambam 9:9 restates this almost word for word, while 9:7 covers a different case of buying wheat in the city versus the village.
B rules on witnesses who saw separately combining (the R. Yehoshua ben Korcha clause), and A rules on testifying at different times (the final clause), so both fit and A is acceptable.
Rambam 28:7 describes squaring the city and then measuring 2000 cubits outside the square on each side, matching the baraita's two-step squaring; B deals with rectangular and round cities.
The line quotes "כדי רשעתו... משום רשעה אחת אתה מחייבו ואי אתה מחייבו משום שתי רשעיות", which appears verbatim in Makkot 13b (B), while A lacks this derivation.
The line explains the one-sixth deficiency (ona'ah) measure for coins, which matches Rambam 12:10 on a sela lacking a sixth; B only covers the time limit for returning.

The line has two parts: deduction of money from the redemption price (Rambam 2:8, A) and the slave acquiring himself with money, money's worth, or a document (Rambam 2:1, B), so both rulings are drawn from it.
The line cites the mishnah on working on Passover eve by local custom, which fits Semag's discussion of labor prohibitions on festivals better than B, a bare heading about Rosh Hashanah.
The line contains both Rav Yehuda's blessing text (SA 219:2) and Abaye and Mar Zutra's ten-and-two-sages requirement with the verse (SA 219:3).
The line says a sick person is not told of a relative's death, no one rends in his presence, and women are silenced; Mourning 8:4 restates exactly this, while 8:5 is about rending for in-laws.
Rava makes the courtyard owner liable for a pit dug by an animal, which is what 410:4 and its Rema gloss rule; 410:5 covers the ox owner's exemption from pit liability, a different point.

The line is Rava's question whether a healthy person who gives all his property to his wife makes her only a steward, and SA 246:2 states exactly that dispute (only a deathbed donor, or a healthy one too), while 246:4 deals with a gift to a son and does not.
The Gemara line lists cases where the debtor admitted or died excommunicated, and SA 130:6 repeats those exact cases (הודה בו, נידוהו ומת בנידויו), while B covers a gentile lender and is unrelated.
The Gemara quotes 'ובא בכל אות נפשו' from Deut 18:6 and 'ושרת' from 18:7, and the cited Deuteronomy 18:6–7 spans both verses, so A is acceptable.

The Steinsaltz and English explicitly cite Leviticus 6:11 ("Whatever shall touch them shall be sacred") as the source for a meal offering being sanctified through absorption, while 7:11 is not quoted.

The Gemara line is the baraita of five sons and five daughters, requiring five gittin each, or four gittin plus ḥalitza if one son died; this is exactly Shulchan Arukh EH 37:19, while 37:20 deals with a father who forgot whom he betrothed his daughter to.
The line's whey and blood exemptions are in 87:6 (A), while its bones, tendons, horns and hooves exemption is in 87:7 (B), so both fit and A is acceptable.
The baraita's list of barren, old, minor, aylonit, sick or imprisoned husband all waiting three months is restated in Rambam 11:20, whereas 11:18 gives only the general waiting rule.
The Gemara quotes "ובשנה הרביעית ובשנה החמישית", which spans Leviticus 19:24 and 19:25, so A (the margin's citation) is acceptable.

judge.reason: The line derives from "ויפל עליו וימת" that exile applies only when the object falls in a downward motion, which is exactly Rambam 6:12; 6:10 covers the hating killer and others who are close to intentional, and says nothing about falling.

The line's procedure (bring it, stay until dark, take it back, then bring and eat it the next day) matches Rambam 8:8 almost verbatim, while 8:9 deals with eating the eiruv on the first day and with eiruv by foot.

The Gemara line says a woman who trades in the house and has bills of sale and documents in her name must prove her claim of inheritance, and Rambam 9:7 restates this nearly verbatim, while 9:8 covers the separate case of brothers dividing the dough.

The line quotes 'ואל פתח אהל מועד לא הביאו' from Lev 17:9, but the offense of offering up a burnt offering or sacrifice is in 17:8, and the Steinsaltz and English quote 17:8–9 together, so A is acceptable.

judge.reason: The Gemara line about ascending or descending an incline and not bending before the gentile is codified in Rambam 12:7, while 12:8 covers widening the road for Esau, which this line does not discuss.

The Gemara line quotes the baraita that spreading kilayim beneath you is permitted by Torah law but forbidden by the Sages lest a fiber wrap around the flesh, which is exactly Rambam 10:12; 10:13 covers soft versus hard materials.

The line has R. Yehuda say the melikah'd bird 'renders impure' like a carcass; Passage A rules a melikah that is invalid (treif, with a knife, or chullin inside/kodashim outside) is a carcass, while B covers disqualified animals and does not fit the context.
Rav Yosef's window, trash heap and palm tree as public thoroughfare is codified in B, while A only restates the mishna's rule about a house open to the public.

The line discusses selling diluted wine in a store and to a merchant even with disclosure, which is exactly the ruling in 228:12; 228:14 concerns a custom of tasting before buying, which the line does not discuss.

The mishna opens with cooking the peace-offering (Rambam 8:2 'ומבשל השלמים או שולקן') and continues with the priest taking the foreleg and waving it (8:4), so both passages draw on this line and A is acceptable.

judge.reason: Halacha 3:13 rules that offerings pinched inside the Temple are pure and not a carcass, which matches the Gemara's derivation from 'nevelah'; B is the neighboring ruling on slaughter and non-sacred birds.
The line quotes "הזכר" from Lev 27:3 and "ואם נקבה היא" from Lev 27:4, so the margin citation to 27:4 is acceptable.

Passage B restates this exact case ("I administer an oath that when you know testimony you will testify for me") as exempt, while A also covers it in its final sentence on an oath preceding the testimony, so A is acceptable.
The Gemara line concerns a gentile collecting a slave for his debt, which Rambam 8:2 codifies word for word ("גבאו עכו"ם בחובו ... לא יצא לחרות"), while 8:3 addresses selling to the king's servants.

judge.reason: The line expounds the verse 'בערכך' (Lev 27:2), which Rambam 1:1 quotes, while 1:8 concerns valuing the sick and healthy alike, a different point.
The Gemara line discusses the rapist's obligation to marry his victim and the ban on divorcing her, and Steinsaltz explicitly cites Deuteronomy 22:29 ("ולו תהיה לאשה... לא יוכל שלחה כל ימיו").
The line sets out blessings on seeing Jewish and gentile sages and kings, which Rambam Blessings 10:11 restates; Blessings 6:11 is about washing hands and has no connection to it.
The Mishnah covers two people holding a knife (Rambam 2:10, A) and also decapitating in one motion and slaughtering two heads at once (Rambam 2:9, B), so A is acceptable.
The Gemara line says a Hebrew slave applies only when the Jubilee is practiced, and Tur YD 267 states this same rule ("אין עבד עברי נוהג אלא בזמן שהיובל נוהג") and discusses it at length.

judge.reason: The line concerns an unrelated woman forbidden as rival wife of a sister via zikah with multiple brothers, which matches the three-brothers case in B rather than A's two-brother case.
The line quotes 'בני אהרן הכהנים' (plural, Lev 1:8), which matches 1:5's wording, whereas 1:7 has singular 'הכהן'.

The line states that next-day intent in the blood, portion, or meat services makes the offering piggul, which is the general rule in Rambam 16:1; B covers the separate case of half-olive-bulk place-intent mixed with time-intent.
The line concerns innards perforated after one siman was slaughtered and ruled tereifa, which is exactly Tur YD 26 (B), not the post-slaughter cutting rules of YD 27.
Sotah 46a uses the same 'ואם נפשך לומר: נאמר כאן... ונאמר להלן' gezeirah shavah formula, but its subject is the heifer's yoke, not the two witnesses of Deut 19.
The line derives liability for each separate bald spot (matching B) and inclusion of the whole head (matching A's 'anywhere on the head'), so both rulings come from it.

The mishna's opening says both buyer and seller are subject to ona'ah, which matches A (12:1, 'both seller and buyer'), and it also says ona'ah applies to a merchant as to a layman, which matches B (12:8); A is acceptable.

The Gemara lists claims such as 'you sold it to me', 'you gave it to me', 'it chased after my cow', 'I found it straying', plus the bailee claims 'unpaid bailee', 'paid bailee' and 'borrower'; B covers the first group and A covers the bailee group, both exempting the one who admits the principal.

The line (Avodah Zarah 21a) says the halakha follows R' Yosei, and Rav Yosef adds 'provided he doesn't make a settlement,' defined as at least three people. Passage B quotes exactly this (Rav Yosef, 'ובלבד שלא יעשה שכונה', no settlement under three), while Passage A discusses other topics (idol nullification, festival days) and does not cover it.

Passage B explicitly discusses whether divorce is like ratification (גירושין כהקמה דמי) and the same-day remarriage case, which is exactly this line's subject, while A deals with the father annulling after an unheard vow.

judge.reason: B codifies the quoted mishna forbidding felling an untrimmed sycamore in Shevi'it, while A gives the cutting heights relevant to the three-handbreadth question in the same line.

The Gemara line bans a leveler made of gourd or metal and permits olive, nut, sycamore and boxwood, which is exactly Rambam Theft 8:5; Theft 8:6 deals with a different matter (shape of the leveler and how it is drawn).
The line cites pus (מוגלא) kosher in the lung but unfit in the kidney, and clear fluid (מים זכין) kosher in both; SA 44:2 rules on exactly these in the kidney, while 44:4 covers only kidney stones.
The line concerns a paternal sister (bat eshet aviv, Lev 18:9–11) born of a forbidden union, which is the subject of Rambam 2:3, not the four forbidden wives in 2:1.
The line quotes 'החדש הזה לכם', which is the opening of Exodus 12:2, while 12:1 only says 'And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron'.
The Gemara's concealed-gift (matana temirta) rule and its 'stam' case underlie both: A gives the ruling on instructions to write or sign publicly, and B applies the stam case, so A is acceptable.
The line's baraita permits those obligated in immersions to immerse on Tisha B'Av, which matches SA 554:8's ruling on mitzvah immersion, while 554:7 covers ordinary bathing.

The line quotes "כדי רשעתו" and the principle "משום רשעה אחת אתה מחייבו, ואי אתה מחייבו משום שתי רשעיות", which appears verbatim in Passage B (R. Yochanan's derivation). Passage A derives a different rule through Ulla's analogies.
The line asks about a hideaway holding only one woman, which Rambam 18:27 (B) rules on explicitly, while 18:28 (A) only explains the general believability of a woman who says she is pure.
The line says witnesses need not rend their clothes because they already did when they heard, which is what Passage B (Mourning 9:8) restates; Passage A is about rending over a burned Torah scroll.
The line says that intending to eat outside the place or outside the time makes the offering invalid with no karet; both Tosefta passages contain 'פסול ואין בו כרת', so both fit and A is acceptable.

Passage A ends by introducing the same baraita of Rabbi Yosei's three elders, and Passage B continues it with Rabbi Yishmael's second-tithe and firstborn argument that the Makkot line quotes, so A is acceptable.
The Gemara quotes Genesis 25:5 and 25:6 as one continuous passage ("ויתן אברהם... ולבני הפילגשים... נתן מתנת"), so a margin citation of 25:5 is acceptable.

The Gemara quotes 'ויבא אל גדרות הצאן על הדרך ושם מערה ויבא שאול להסך את רגליו', which is the text of passage B (I Samuel 24:4 in this numbering), while passage A is about Saul taking three thousand men.

alt: Mishneh Torah, Daily Offerings and Additional Offerings 9:13

judge.reason: The opening clause (precedence in sacrifice means precedence in eating) matches A, while the yesterday/today peace offering and sin/guilt offering cases match B.

ref: Mishneh Torah, Prayer and the Priestly Blessing 14:6

judge.reason: Rambam 14:6 states the same law as Rav Hisda's first statement: priests may not bend their finger joints until they turn their faces away from the congregation.

The Gemara line gives the exceptions (plaintiff or witnesses ill, witnesses about to travel overseas, defendant summoned and did not come), which is exactly the content of 28:16; 28:15 gives only the general rule that testimony is not accepted in the defendant's absence.
The line limits the olive-bulk measure to edible items, as Ravina does in 25a ('מידי דבר אכילה'), while 28b is about oaths on ten/nine and figs/grapes, which is unrelated.
Shulchan Arukh YD 384:1 codifies the baraita's prohibition on a mourner studying Torah, Prophets, Writings, Mishnah, halakhot and aggadot, with the exception when the public needs him.
The Tur says 'מאימתי חזרת משחקי בקוביא משישברו כליהם... דאפילו בחנם לא עבדי', which restates this Gemara line's ruling on when dice players' repentance counts.
The line turns on who counts as a zona (not a raped woman), which is the definition in 18:1; 18:8 deals with believing a claim of rape, not this question.
The line covers both pain (burning a fingernail with a skewer, Passage B) and medical costs (a drug that whitened the flesh, Passage A), so the margin's citation of A is acceptable.

The line quotes the mishna that shards of vessels may be moved if they serve a similar function (bowl shards covering a barrel, glass shards covering a cruse), which is what Rambam 25:12 codifies; 25:13 covers vessel covers and does not address this.

Passage A covers the wife's vow with the husband adding 'and I', which he cannot annul because that would be confirmation; Passage B covers 'I am a nazirite and you' with 'amen' and the reverse case, so both are drawn from this line.
